overview:
Interfaith participation, within a Jain studies framework, refers to the respectful, non‑coercive engagement of Jains with individuals and communities of other religious traditions. It includes dialogue, shared ethical initiatives, academic collaboration, and participation in civic or humanitarian programs. Jain traditions—Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrti‑pūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth—have historically interacted with diverse communities across South Asia, often emphasizing ahiṃsā (non‑violence), anekāntavāda (many‑sidedness), and aparigraha (non‑possessiveness) as guiding principles.

From a foundations perspective, interfaith participation is not framed as doctrinal compromise but as an application of anekāntavāda: the recognition that truth is complex and that differing viewpoints may contain partial insights. Classical Jain texts do not explicitly describe modern interfaith forums, but they provide conceptual tools for respectful engagement. Medieval commentaries and modern scholarship highlight how Jain communities have historically collaborated with Buddhists, Hindus, and later Muslims and Christians in matters of ethics, trade, and civic life.

In contemporary practice, interfaith participation often involves Jains contributing perspectives on non‑violence, environmental stewardship, vegetarianism, and peaceful coexistence. Lay organizations may join interfaith councils, humanitarian projects, or academic panels. However, Jain ethics emphasize voluntary participation, non‑harm, and avoidance of coercion. Participation must not conflict with core vows, and individuals are encouraged to seek guidance from qualified teachers when unsure about ritual boundaries.

Across traditions, interfaith participation is seen as an opportunity to cultivate maitri (friendliness) and pramoda (appreciation), while maintaining clarity about Jain identity and commitments. Modern Jain leaders frequently encourage dialogue that is grounded in humility, non‑violence, and intellectual openness, while avoiding syncretism that erases doctrinal distinctions.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation: Because of the doctrine of many‑sidedness, truth has multiple aspects.
primary_sources.notes: This is a paraphrased thematic line rather than a verbatim sutra; the Tattvārtha Sūtra articulates anekāntavāda across several passages (notably TS 1.6–1.33). The concept is foundational for interfaith engagement, as it supports respectful recognition of diverse viewpoints.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Mahāvīra’s disciples
primary_sources.notes: This early Śvetāmbara canonical text emphasizes universal compassion, forming an ethical basis for peaceful coexistence and respectful interreligious interaction.

primary_sources.title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.translation: The essence of knowledge is its many‑sidedness.
primary_sources.notes: This passage reinforces the epistemic humility central to Jain engagement with differing viewpoints.

misconceptions.myth: Jainism discourages any interaction with other religions.
misconceptions.reality: Jain ethics emphasize non‑violence, humility, and respect. Interfaith participation is acceptable when it does not compromise core vows or involve coercive ritual participation.

misconceptions.myth: Anekāntavāda means all religions are identical.
misconceptions.reality: Anekāntavāda teaches that truth is many‑sided, not that all doctrines are the same. It encourages respectful dialogue while maintaining clear Jain philosophical commitments.

misconceptions.myth: Interfaith participation requires adopting practices from other traditions.
misconceptions.reality: Jain participation is voluntary and non‑syncretic. Jains may join ethical or civic initiatives without adopting external rituals or beliefs.
